items.text: a bridge woven from spider silk and vines
a chair that scratches the sitter's back with wooden fingers
a rain-catching roof made entirely of enormous leaves
a wooden device that turns itself off whenever someone starts it
a special frame intended to force coconuts to grow square
a cart that is pulled by snails
a hollow coconut meant to catch rain before it falls
a statue designed to frighten storms away
a writing system made entirely of pictures of frogs
a tree planted upside down to make its fruit easier to pick
a machine for teaching fish to climb trees
a stone wheel with corners, "so it won't roll away"
a basket that can carry itself downhill but not uphill
a pair of sandals with little umbrellas for each toe
a bell that rings whenever the village is too noisy
a device for stirring soup using the motion of a goat's tail
a very long spoon for eating from someone else's bowl
a rope ladder that is longer at the top than at the bottom
a new kind of door that can only be opened when it is already open
a water wheel placed on dry land "to save water"

intro.name: The exhibition
intro.text:
The village has agreed to hold an exhibition of new inventions. (Subject), a notoriously imaginative researcher, arrives carrying a bundle of sketches so large that (subject.he/she) cannot see over it. (Friend), a practical builder, offers to help sort the proposals.
"I have discovered seventeen ways to improve village life," announces (Subject). "Have you tested any of them?" asks (Friend).
"Of course not! That would spoil the surprise."

question.name: The first proposal
question.text: The first proposal is {IDEA}. The villagers must decide how to respond.

choices.label: Give the inventor supplies for a small, supervised test.
Invite everyone to vote on the idea.
Ask the inventor to explain exactly what problem it solves.

a1.name: A1
a1.text: The villagers gather expecting disaster. Instead, the little contraption works beautifully. The bridge holds a basket of stones; the leaf roof keeps a bench dry; or the wooden mechanism performs its humble task without breaking. (Friend) checks the result twice. "Well," (friend.he/she) says, "I owe you an apology." (Subject) folds (subject.his/her) arms. "I shall accept it in the form of more materials." The village agrees to improve the design before using it for anything important.

a2.name: A2
a2.text: The device works exactly as (Subject) promised. It turns itself off, rings when someone shouts, or moves a stone from one side of a table to the other. Everyone waits for the useful part. "That is the useful part," (Subject) explains. "But why?" asks (Friend). "Because now we know it can be done." The council awards the invention a certificate for TECHNICAL SUCCESS AND COMPLETE PRACTICAL IRRELEVANCE.

a3.name: A3
a3.text: After three days of work, the contraption collapses into a heap of vines, wood, and broken shells. (Subject) stares at the wreckage. "The theory was sound," (subject.he/she) says. "The legs weren't," replies (Friend). The council orders that future demonstrations use scraps before consuming precious supplies. (Subject) calls the rule oppressive. The farmers call it sensible.

text_only.reason: the invention falls apart, not one of the game's structures

a4.name: A4
a4.text: The invention fails magnificently. While trying to repair it, however, (Friend) notices that a particular knot holds far more weight than the others. The builders test the knot, improve it, and teach it to the village. (Subject) claims credit for the discovery. (Friend) points out that the original machine was supposed to teach fish to climb trees. "And yet," (Subject) replies, "look how far science has come."

a5.name: A5
a5.text: The cart moves! The crowd cheers! The snails continue moving with magnificent determination. By sundown, the cart has advanced the width of a coconut. (Subject) announces that the transportation problem has been solved. (Friend) asks how long a journey to the other side of the village would take. (Subject) requests several weeks to calculate the answer.

a6.name: A6
a6.text: (Subject) unveils a new writing system containing sixty-three drawings of frogs. "This symbol means harvest," (subject.he/she) explains. "And this one means rain." (Friend) points to a third frog. "What does that mean?" (Subject) hesitates. "I forgot." The villagers vote to keep their existing writing system. One child, however, begins using the frog symbols to pass secret messages to friends. Within a week, the children understand it better than its inventor.

a7.name: A7
a7.text: (Subject) plants a young tree with its roots pointing toward the sky. "Now the fruit will grow underground where we can reach it!" (subject.he/she) announces. The farmers gently explain that roots are not merely branches with poor ambition. (Subject) is unconvinced until the tree begins to wilt. The farmers replant it properly. "Perhaps," (Subject) admits, "trees have strong opinions about which way is up."

a8.name: A8
a8.text: The invention almost works. Then it almost works again. By the seventh attempt, (Subject) has announced seven separate breakthroughs, none of which have occurred. (Friend) suggests stopping for the day. "But the next test could change everything!" (Subject) protests. "Then it can change everything tomorrow," replies (Friend). The council establishes a sensible limit on how long one person may occupy the workshop.

b1.name: B1
b1.text: The villagers vote overwhelmingly against the invention. (Subject) is stunned. "You have rejected the future!" (subject.he/she) cries. An elder points out that the future may return with a better design. (Subject) vows to do just that, but only after giving a long speech about how history will remember this injustice. Nobody stays for the entire speech.

b2.name: B2
b2.text: Every adult votes against the invention. Every child votes for it. The children win by a single vote after an elderly villager changes (elder.his/her) mind, saying that a frog-shaped rain catcher would brighten the village. (Subject) is delighted. (Friend) insists that the first version be small, cheap, and harmless. It becomes the most beloved useless object in Isola.

b3.name: B3
b3.text: The crowd loves the idea. The builders, who must actually construct it, do not. "A bridge of spider silk!" cries one admirer. "A masterpiece!" "Have you ever tried collecting enough spider silk to make a bridge?" asks (Friend). The admirer has not. After a long argument, the council approves a miniature demonstration instead. The tiny bridge holds one pebble. Everyone cheers as though an entire river has been crossed.

b4.name: B4
b4.text: (Subject) wins the vote by a suspicious margin. Investigation reveals that (subject.he/she) has submitted several ballots under the names of (subject.his/her) inventions. "THE GREAT RAIN CATCHER IS A STAKEHOLDER!" (subject.he/she) protests. The council voids the extra ballots and orders a fair vote. (Subject) accepts the ruling with the dignity of someone who has been caught very publicly cheating at something extremely silly.

b5.name: B5
b5.text: The vote is evenly divided. The council asks (Subject) to explain the idea once more. After the explanation, three supporters change their votes to "no," four opponents change theirs to "yes," and one villager announces that (villager.he/she) no longer understands what a coconut is. The council postpones the decision. (Subject) calls this a historic victory.

b6.name: B6
b6.text: The crowd laughs until a respected elder rises. "I remember when people laughed at the first person who tried to carry water in a woven vessel," (elder.he/she) says. "This idea may be dreadful. But laughter is not proof." The council agrees to test a small version. (Subject) thanks the elder, then immediately proposes a second invention involving upside-down goats. The elder sits down again.

b7.name: B7
b7.text: After hours of arguing, the villagers vote not on the invention but on whether (Subject) should be allowed to speak at the next meeting. The motion passes, narrowly. (Subject) takes the result as evidence that the village fears (subject.his/her) genius. (Friend) quietly suggests that speeches should be shorter than the inventions they describe.

c1.name: C1
c1.text: "To make work easier," says (Subject). (Friend) asks whose work. (Subject) looks at the drawing. "Mine, obviously." It turns out the contraption would save (Subject) ten steps each morning while requiring two other villagers to operate it all day. The council declines the proposal. (Subject) complains that nobody appreciates efficiency.

c2.name: C2
c2.text: (Subject) explains the problem clearly, demonstrates a simple model, and shows exactly how much labor the invention might save. (Friend), prepared for nonsense, is startled. "Why didn't you say all that at the start?"

c2_2.name: C2
c2_2.text: "Because," says (Subject), "I thought the dramatic unveiling would be more impressive." The council approves a cautious trial. For once, the most ridiculous-looking proposal has a perfectly sensible purpose.

c3.name: C3
c3.text: (Subject) begins with the history of coconuts, proceeds to the movement of the stars, and somehow arrives at the mating habits of crabs. Three hours later, (Friend) interrupts. "WHAT DOES THE MACHINE DO?" (Subject) pauses. "I was just getting to that." The meeting is adjourned before sunset.

c4.name: C4
c4.text: "It solves the problem of meaning," (Subject) announces. (Friend) studies the wooden box. "How?" "By proving that even an apparently useless thing can have a purpose." "And what is its purpose?" "To prove that." (Friend) rubs (friend.his/her) temples. The village's philosophers are delighted. The builders are not.

c5.name: C5
c5.text: (Subject) stares at the drawings for a long time. "I don't know," (subject.he/she) finally says. The admission surprises everyone, including (Subject). Instead of laughing, (Friend) asks which part of the idea first seemed interesting. Together they identify a smaller question worth testing. (Subject) goes home with fewer grand plans and one genuinely good one.

c6.name: C6
c6.text: The crowd bursts into laughter as (Subject) explains the device. (Subject) does not laugh. "I worked on this for months," (subject.he/she) says quietly. The room grows uncomfortable. (Friend) apologizes for the ridicule, then explains the actual flaws in the design. (Subject) listens, still hurt, but asks for help improving it. The invention may never work. The apology still matters.

c7.name: C7
c7.text: (Subject) solemnly announces a new device for carrying water without getting wet. It is a bowl. (Friend) stares. The council stares. (Subject) maintains a perfectly serious expression until an elder begins explaining how bowls work. Then (Subject) collapses with laughter. "I HAVE BEEN WAITING ALL WEEK FOR SOMEONE TO SAY THAT!" (subject.he/she) wheezes. The council bans practical jokes from the next invention fair. The children immediately begin planning their entries.

c8.name: C8
c8.text: (Subject) admits that the machine is impossible as drawn. "But what if we used the same arrangement of vines to lift a heavy stone?" asks (Friend). The builders try it. To everyone's surprise, the arrangement works. The original invention is abandoned, and a useful lifting frame takes its place. (Subject) watches the first stone rise and grins. "I told you my ridiculous ideas might work." "One part of one idea," (Friend) corrects. "I SHALL TAKE IT!" replies (Subject).
